title: The Tyranny of Shipyard Cost-Plus Contracting
gist: The commander of Norfolk Naval Shipyard argues that cost-plus and level-of-effort contracting for private-sector work inside public shipyards rewards labor consumption over completion, and is an underexamined cause of the maintenance delays that cost attack submarines 15,000 operational days and $3.4 billion over a decade. He argues the contract vehicle is industrial-base strategy: labor-hour reimbursement makes adding workers more profitable than automating, and the Navy should pay for uncertainty only while uncertainty exists.

themes.theme: The Scale of the Maintenance Problem

insights.claim: A recent GAO report found that over the past 10 years maintenance delays for attack submarines produced 15,000 lost operational days and an estimated $3.4 billion in costs.
insights.speaker: Kavon Hakimzadeh
insights.so_what: Quantifies the readiness gap in both time and dollars — the number Congress and shipbuilders will anchor to in any submarine industrial base funding debate.
insights.quote: over the past 10 years, maintenance delays for attack submarines have resulted in 15,000 lost operational days and an estimated $3.4 billion in costs
insights.locator: Public shipyard availabilities

insights.claim: Public shipyards rely heavily on private vendors: as of writing, the Navy had contracted out half of an aircraft carrier availability and just over 30 percent of a submarine availability at Norfolk Naval Shipyard.
insights.speaker: Kavon Hakimzadeh
insights.so_what: Sizes the revenue stream flowing to private ship-repair firms through public-yard subcontracts — the segment most exposed to any contracting-model reform.
insights.quote: the Navy has contracted out half of an aircraft carrier availability and just over 30 percent of a submarine availability to private vendors at Norfolk Naval Shipyard
insights.locator: Because of traditionally high volumes of work

insights.claim: Work placed at a private shipyard typically ends in a firm-fixed-price contract, while private-sector work performed inside public shipyards is instead structured as cost-plus or level-of-effort largely out of convenience — a distinction rarely made in public debate.
insights.speaker: Kavon Hakimzadeh
insights.so_what: Isolates a specific, narrow contracting venue as the problem — meaning reform is targeted and does not require overhauling all Navy ship-repair contracting.
insights.quote: For a variety of reasons — largely convenience — this is not the case for private-sector work at public shipyards.
insights.locator: It is important to emphasize that this is not a discussion

insights.claim: Cost-plus and level-of-effort contracting reward labor consumption over timely completion, misaligning private-sector economics with the operational imperative of returning ships to the fleet.
insights.speaker: Kavon Hakimzadeh
insights.so_what: The core mechanism: schedule delay is not a contractor failure under these terms, it is the economically rational outcome the terms produce.
insights.quote: Instead, they can reward labor consumption over timely completion.
insights.locator: Cost-plus contracting reimburses contractors

insights.claim: The real problem with cost-plus is not that contractors earn more when costs rise — a fixed fee means their effective fee percentage falls — but that they do not bear the downside risk of cost growth, which the government absorbs.
insights.speaker: Kavon Hakimzadeh
insights.so_what: Corrects a common misdiagnosis: the issue is risk allocation, not profiteering, which points reform toward risk-transfer structures rather than fee caps.
insights.quote: The concern on the deckplates is not that a contractor necessarily makes more profit when costs increase.
insights.locator: The Perverse Math of the Fee

insights.claim: On a $10 million cost-plus repair with a $700,000 fixed fee, efficient performance at $8 million raises the effective fee to 8.75 percent while cost growth to $15 million cuts it to roughly 4.7 percent — yet the government, not the contractor, pays the extra $5 million.
insights.speaker: Kavon Hakimzadeh
insights.so_what: A worked numerical example showing the contractor stays financially whole through overruns — the arithmetic behind the persistent schedule slippage.
insights.quote: The contractor remains financially whole because the Navy is effectively footing the bill to “keep the lights on.”
insights.locator: The Perverse Math of the Fee

insights.claim: Level-of-effort contracts buy labor hours rather than completed outcomes, and become dangerous when used as a substitute for defining work through rigorous planning rather than for genuinely undefinable maintenance.
insights.speaker: Kavon Hakimzadeh
insights.so_what: Distinguishes legitimate from abusive use of the same instrument — the test any oversight review should apply to an availability's contract mix.
insights.quote: But level-of-effort becomes dangerous when it is used as a substitute for defining work through rigorous planning.
insights.locator: Definitized Work vs. Level of Effort

insights.claim: The real trap springs when growth work is discovered in drydock and the administrative 'easy button' is to add funding to an existing level-of-effort structure rather than scope and definitize the new requirement.
insights.speaker: Kavon Hakimzadeh
insights.so_what: Identifies the precise decision point where availabilities become open-ended — the intervention target for any process reform.
insights.quote: Over time, this creates a black hole of accountability.
insights.locator: The real trap springs when growth work is discovered

insights.claim: The purpose of contracting in an availability is to shape vendor behavior, not to compensate for slow internal decision-making, so the objection that definitizing work slows availabilities confuses contracting discipline with government process inefficiency.
insights.speaker: Kavon Hakimzadeh
insights.so_what: Pre-empts the standard institutional defense of level-of-effort and relocates the fix to internal decision authority rather than the contract vehicle.
insights.quote: The purpose of contracting in an availability is to shape vendor behavior, not to compensate for slow internal decision-making.
insights.locator: Critics may argue that this kind of rigor

insights.claim: In ship maintenance, all parties associated with an availability should treat time as an independent variable rather than as a residual that absorbs every other delay.
insights.speaker: Kavon Hakimzadeh
insights.so_what: A one-line management principle that, if adopted, changes which party bears schedule risk across every Navy maintenance contract.
insights.quote: In ship maintenance, all parties associated with an availability should treat time as an independent variable.
insights.locator: If the Navy wants outcome-based contracts to work

insights.claim: The Navy's contracting model determines what the private ship-repair industrial base invests in, how it organizes its workforce and how aggressively it pursues productivity — it does more than allocate work.
insights.speaker: Kavon Hakimzadeh
insights.so_what: Reframes contract structure as the primary lever on private capital allocation in ship repair — more consequential than direct industrial-base subsidies.
insights.quote: It helps drive efficiency by determining what the private ship-repair industrial base chooses to invest in, how it organizes its workforce, and how aggressively it pursues productivity.
insights.locator: Contracting Is Industrial Base Strategy

insights.claim: Under labor-hour reimbursement, a contractor that could spend $1 million on robotic welding or digital work instructions to cut $2 million of labor has no incentive to do so, because the technology destroys the revenue base — and this holds regardless of how much competition exists.
insights.speaker: Kavon Hakimzadeh
insights.so_what: Explains structurally why shipyard automation and advanced manufacturing adoption has lagged — competition alone will not fix it, only contract structure will.
insights.quote: But under a labor-driven reimbursement model, the technology reduces the very labor hours from which revenue is generated.
insights.locator: Consider a contractor that could invest $1 million

insights.claim: Simply adding more labor to an inefficient production model will not solve the Navy's ship-repair capacity problem; the requirement is to increase throughput per worker, per dock, and per dollar.
insights.speaker: Kavon Hakimzadeh
insights.so_what: Productivity, not headcount, is the binding constraint — which favors automation and process-technology suppliers over pure staffing growth.
insights.quote: Simply adding more labor to an inefficient production model will not solve the capacity problem.
insights.locator: This is critical as the Navy attempts to expand repair capacity

insights.claim: Under an appropriately structured fixed-price or incentive arrangement the contractor retains a portion of savings, making productivity and long-term capital investment highly profitable.
insights.speaker: Kavon Hakimzadeh
insights.so_what: The mechanism that would unlock private capex in ship repair — watch for incentive-structure language in new Navy solicitations as the leading indicator.
insights.quote: the contractor retains a portion of the savings, making productivity and long-term capital investments highly profitable
insights.locator: Under an appropriately structured fixed-price

insights.claim: Cost-plus and level-of-effort should be used deliberately but only temporarily during the early rip-out and inspection phases, after which the Navy should definitize the work and shift as much as practical to firm-fixed-price or fixed-price incentive structures.
insights.speaker: Kavon Hakimzadeh
insights.so_what: A phased risk-transfer model that a sitting shipyard commander is publicly advocating — a concrete reform proposal that could show up in future contracting policy.
insights.quote: Put simply, the Navy should pay for uncertainty only while uncertainty exists — and stop paying for it once that uncertainty has been resolved.
insights.locator: Breaking the Cycle

insights.claim: Portions of public shipyard availabilities such as hull preservation or defined combat-system upgrades could be broken into logical definitized work packages and competed among qualified vendors using fixed-price or incentive-based task orders.
insights.speaker: Kavon Hakimzadeh
insights.so_what: Names the specific work categories most likely to be competitively re-bid — where new entrants and specialized vendors could win share.
insights.locator: The Navy should also consider breaking appropriate portions

insights.claim: In thin markets such as submarine combat systems work, pushing maximum performance risk onto a single qualified contractor through firm-fixed-price is a recipe for poor outcomes, since vendors will either price in large defensive risk premiums or decline to bid.
insights.speaker: Kavon Hakimzadeh
insights.so_what: A caution that aggressive fixed-price reform can accelerate vendor exit in specialized niches — the failure mode to watch if the Navy overcorrects.
insights.quote: In a thin market, pushing maximum performance risk onto a single-qualified contractor through firm-fixed-price contracts is a recipe for poor outcomes.
insights.locator: The Single-Source Risk

insights.claim: In sole-source environments the Navy should use negotiated fixed-price incentive (firm target) structures with a realistic target cost, target profit and clear sharing of overruns and underruns up to a negotiated ceiling, functioning as a structured partnership.
insights.speaker: Kavon Hakimzadeh
insights.so_what: The specific contract type being advocated for fragile single-vendor niches — a middle path that protects suppliers while transferring some risk.
insights.quote: If the contractor innovates and beats the target, they make more profit — if they encounter inefficiencies, they share the financial pain up to a negotiated ceiling.
insights.locator: In these single-source environments

insights.claim: The Navy's implementation of multiple-award indefinite-delivery, indefinite-quantity contracts has already reduced the thin-market problem, though it may persist in specialized areas.
insights.speaker: Kavon Hakimzadeh
insights.so_what: Indicates a partially built vendor pool already exists, lowering the practical barrier to competing fixed-price task orders in most work categories.
insights.locator: The Single-Source Risk

insights.claim: Shipyards sit at the nexus of risk transfer between the Navy's technical community, which delivers late-breaking ship change documents after planning windows close, and the operational community, which demands ever-shorter availabilities.
insights.speaker: Kavon Hakimzadeh
insights.so_what: The structural explanation for persistent reform failure — pressure comes from two directions that neither the shipyard nor the contracting officer controls.
insights.quote: Both public and private shipyards lie squarely at the nexus of risk transfer between the Navy’s technical and operational communities.
insights.locator: The Nexus of Risk — Why Change Is Hard

insights.claim: When late technical changes collide with compressed operational schedules, contracting officers lose the time to inspect, scope and negotiate fixed-price vehicles, so the system defaults to cost-plus or level-of-effort to get workers on the job immediately.
insights.speaker: Kavon Hakimzadeh
insights.so_what: Reform requires giving contracting officers schedule slack upfront — without that, the default will persist regardless of policy guidance.
insights.quote: It is the administrative survival mechanism for a workforce trapped between demands for technical precision and operational speed.
insights.locator: When late technical changes collide

insights.claim: Asking contractors to absorb execution risk will produce higher initial bids, since they will price that risk into their proposals.
insights.speaker: Kavon Hakimzadeh
insights.so_what: Expect headline unit costs on ship repair to rise before total cost falls — a near-term optics problem that could stall reform politically.
insights.quote: when contractors are asked to absorb execution risk, they will price that risk into their proposals, resulting in higher initial bids
insights.locator: Readiness Through Accountability

insights.claim: Pushing too much downside risk too quickly onto a fragile ship-repair industrial base could drive smaller specialized vendors out of the defense market entirely, destroying the capacity the Navy is trying to nurture.
insights.speaker: Kavon Hakimzadeh
insights.so_what: Sequencing risk: aggressive fixed-price conversion is a credible route to consolidation and reduced capacity in the ship-repair supplier base.
insights.quote: the current ship-repair industrial base is fragile
insights.locator: Readiness Through Accountability

insights.claim: Fixed-price models create their own behavioral risks — temptation to cut corners on quality when margin is threatened by a ceiling, and adversarial claim-driven relationships if the Navy fix-prices poorly definitized work.
insights.speaker: Kavon Hakimzadeh
insights.so_what: Fixed-price conversion requires intensified government oversight spend and rigorous scoping — the hidden cost that determines whether reform actually saves money.
insights.quote: Instead of repairing ships, Navy project teams and vendors will spend their time fighting over technical interpretations and requests for equitable adjustment.
insights.locator: Similarly, if the Navy attempts to fix-price work
